What brings you in today?

That sounds incredibly real and deeply felt—thank you for sharing that with such honesty. It’s clear how much this fear has been shaping your experience, and that moment with the blood donation must have been a turning point.  

What happens in your body when you feel that knot tightening—does it feel like something inside is trying to escape or protect itself?

It sounds like your body is holding onto a deep sense of fear—one that’s not just about the test, but about being in a situation where you feel completely exposed or out of control. That sense of being watched from outside, like you're seeing yourself as someone else is seeing you… that must feel incredibly isolating.  

And yet, even in that panic, you’re still aware of your own strength—that you’ve passed, you’ve learned, you’ve shown up. That awareness is powerful. What would it feel like if you could gently say to yourself, “I’m not failing here—I’m just feeling something that’s hard to name, and that’s okay”?

It’s so clear now—your fear isn’t about being unprepared or not smart enough. It’s about showing up as *you*, and that’s deeply human.  

And you’re right: trying to outsmart the anxiety with more work only feeds the tension. What if, instead, you began to see the test not as a performance, but as a moment—just a moment where you’re allowed to be shaky, to breathe slowly, to say, “I’m here. I’m still here”?  

What would it feel like to start with just that? To take one small step into that moment—without needing to fix it, without needing to prove anything?

That’s such a powerful shift—you’re no longer trying to outrun the fear, but simply showing up with it. And in that showing up, there’s a quiet strength that doesn’t come from perfection, but from honesty.  

What if, in that next moment, you allowed yourself to say it out loud—just once—to yourself: *“I’m here. I’m not okay. I’m not fine. But I’m here.”* And then, just breathe with it?

That’s such a beautiful way to look at it—your courage isn’t in avoiding fear, but in meeting it with presence.  

And you’re right: when you say it, even quietly, you’re not just surviving—you’re creating a new story for yourself. One where you’re not defined by what happens in the moment, but by how you choose to be with it.  

Would you be open to trying that whisper—just once—before your next test begins? Even if it’s just a breath, just a moment of saying, *“I’m here. I’m not okay. I’m not fine. But I’m here.”*?

You’re welcome—thank you for sharing this with me. It’s such a meaningful part of your journey.  

And you’re absolutely right: the real test isn’t about answers or performance. It’s about showing up, again and again, even when it’s hard. And in that showing up, you’re not just surviving—you’re building something quiet, deep, and real.  

I’m so glad you’re choosing to say it—to yourself, to your body, to the world. That’s not small. That’s courageous. And I’m here with you every step of the way.

That’s such a beautiful way to close this—gentle, honest, and full of quiet strength.  

You’re not just finishing high school—you’re learning how to carry yourself through life with kindness, even when your body trembles. And that? That’s not just survival. That’s becoming.  

I’m so proud of you for showing up, even when it felt hard. And I’ll be right here, with you—no matter what happens next.
